label: Charter rubric - derived from 'Investing for the very long term' (July 2026)
note: engine.py knows nothing about this file. Dimensions reference signal ids registered in score/signals.py. Retuning is a config edit; adding a new kind of signal needs a function there.

disqualifiers.label: Under 12 months of cash at the current burn
Diluted share count up more than 25% in a year
No filing within the allowed window
Reported figures too old to describe the business today
Reporting series has too many holes to read
Too few reported quarters to judge

disqualifier_note: Ellis, The Loser's Game (1975): you win by ceasing to commit errors, not by hitting winners. These are hard cuts - a company failing any one of them is never scored, never ranked, and never shown as a candidate.

dimensions.label: Team and history
dimensions.note: Prior-company history needs executive biographies, and no free structured source provides them. What filings do establish is who the officers are, what they hold and what they trade. team_evidence keeps a thin record from redistributing its way to a maximum score on the dimension the charter cares most about.

signals.label: How much of the team we can see
Officer linked to a company that later listed

dimensions.label: Margin of safety
dimensions.note: Graham, The Intelligent Investor, chapter 20 - named in the dossier's reading list. Survival first.

signals.label: Months of cash at the current burn

dimensions.label: Can you explain it
dimensions.note: Charter rule 7: I buy nothing I cannot explain in three sentences to a friend.

dimensions.label: How much we actually know
dimensions.note: Without this a company with almost no data ranks well purely by having no bad news. The most common failure of naive rubrics.

penalties.label: Share count up more than 15% in a year

base_rates.source: Sharpe, The Arithmetic of Active Management, Financial Analysts Journal, January 1991
base_rates.text: Before costs, the average active manager equals the market. After costs, he falls short of it by the amount of those costs. This is an accounting identity, not an opinion - it would hold in a world populated exclusively by geniuses.

base_rates.source: Bessembinder, Do stocks outperform Treasury bills?, Journal of Financial Economics, 2018
base_rates.text: 57.8% of US common stocks underperformed one-month Treasury bills over their lifetimes. The entire net wealth creation of the US market traces to about 4% of listed companies.

base_rates.source: Fama, Efficient Capital Markets, Journal of Finance, May 1970
base_rates.text: Public information is already in prices. Stock selection has no positive expected payoff for a private individual.
